title: Why your friends have more friends than you
description:
In 2011 Facebook measured 721 million users: 92.7% had fewer friends than the average of their friends. Nobody is lying. Popular people sit on many friend lists, so when you average your friends' friend counts, the popular ones get counted again and again. In the six-person group in the video, the average person has 2 friends but the average friend has 3, and five of the six people lose the comparison. Sociologist Scott Feld named it in 1991: the friendship paradox.

Numbers checked in code: the six-person group, plus 200,000 simulated picks of a random friendship (average friend 3.00) and 2,000 random networks (the average friend never had fewer friends than the average person). Sources: Ugander, Karrer, Backstrom, Marlow, 'The Anatomy of the Facebook Social Graph' (2011, arXiv 1111.4503); Feld, 'Why your friends have more friends than you do', American Journal of Sociology (1991).

beats.say: Your friends have more friends than you do.
On Facebook, that's true for 93% of people. And it's not because you're boring.
It's a counting trick. Take six people. Max knows everyone. Ana and Ben know each other. Cleo, Dev and Eli only know Max.
Count friends. Max has 5. Ana and Ben, 2. The rest, 1.
Now compare, like you do online. Cleo has 1. Her friend has 5. Ana has 2. Her friends average 3.5.
Five of six people lose. Only Max wins. So who's cheating?
Max is on five friend lists. Cleo is on one. So Max gets counted five times.
The average person here has 2 friends. The average friend has 3. Popular people are in everyone's list.
